issues.title: `Body` related parameters don't take `alias` in consideration
issues.body: ### Privileged issue - [X] I'm @tiangolo or he asked me directly to create an issue here. ### Issue Content The `Body`, `File`, and `Form` parameters don't support `alias`. The following snippet demonstrates the issue: ```py from typing import Annotated from fastapi import Body, Cookie, FastAPI, Form, UploadFile, File, Query, Header, Path app = FastAPI() @app.post("/{path}") def endpoint( path: Annotated[int, Path(alias="PathAlias")], cookie: Annotated[int, Cookie(alias="CookieAlias")], header: Annotated[int, Header(alias="HeaderAlias")], query: Annotated[int, Query(alias="QueryAlias")], body: Annotated[int, Body(alias="BodyAlias")], form: Annotated[int, Form(alias="FormAlias")], file: Annotated[UploadFile, File(alias="FileAlias")], ): ... ``` If you look at the generated Swagger you see that `alias` is only being used for `params.Param` related fields i.e. `Path`, `Cookie`, etc. People can overcome this right now using `validation_alias` as follows: ```py from typing import Annotated from fastapi import Body, Cookie, FastAPI, Form, UploadFile, File, Query, Header, Path app = FastAPI() @app.post("/{path}") def endpoint( path: Annotated[int, Path(alias="PathAlias")], cookie: Annotated[int, Cookie(alias="CookieAlias")], header: Annotated[int, Header(alias="HeaderAlias")], query: Annotated[int, Query(alias="QueryAlias")], body: Annotated[int, Body(validation_alias="BodyAlias")], form: Annotated[int, Form(validation_alias="FormAlias")], file: Annotated[UploadFile, File(validation_alias="FileAlias")], ): ... ``` In any case, this should be fixed in FastAPI.

### Issue Content

Although I have not contacted tiangolo, I received [an approval](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/discussions/9709#discussioncomment-6498728) from @Kludex to create an issue for this.

Right now there is a problem with how FastAPI handles `RequestValidationError` when a `list` query parameter is empty with Pydantic v2. Quoting Kludex's original comment:

> This is a bug.

> It's not related to UUID, but with any list:

> 
> if __name__ == "__main__":
>     import uvicorn

>     uvicorn.run(f"{__name__}:app", reload=True)

issues.title: Why does APIRouter not allow extra keyword args to be passed along to a route class?
issues.body:
How come there is no way to pass any extra data down through the route decorators to a custom route class.

This seems like a small addition for what could be a very useful feature? Is there a reason this has not been done.

```
@router.get("/", some_extra_info = 1)
def get_something(): ...
```

Storing this in, say, a `route_extra` dict would allow you to do something like

`if router.routes[0].route_extra.get("some_extra_info") == 1: ...`

The only way to do this currently is to duplicate (since these classes are rather inextensible by nature) `APIRouter` and `APIRoute`.

The change would be rather trivial, of only adding a **kwds parameter to each of the decorators and appropriate methods, and add to the APIRoute class a new public property called extra_data which receives this.

```py
from __future__ import annotations

import http
import logging

from fastapi import FastAPI


app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/", status_code=http.HTTPStatus.NO_CONTENT)
async def root() -> None:
    logging.info("endpoint called.")
```

issues.title: Migrate questions in GitHub Issues to GitHub Discussions
issues.body:
### Privileged issue - [X] I'm @tiangolo or he asked me directly to create an issue here. ### Issue Content This is just to describe the process of migrating the GitHub issues with questions (with the label `question`) to GitHub Discussions. Not sure if this would be useful to anyone else, maybe just for me to come back to this if I ever need it. :shrug: ## Current GitHub Support GitHub currently has a feature to migrate issues with a label to GitHub Discussions. What it does is: * For each open issue with that label, create the equivalent discussion, with all the comments, by the same users, etc. * The issue still exists, apart from the discussion, but is then closed and locked. And the UI shows a link to the one in GitHub Discussions. * This information, the fact that it was migrated and that there's now a corresponding discussion, is not available in the APIs (not in REST, not in GraphQL). * An alternative that worked in my case, but not necessarily in others, is to check for locked issues. This worked for me only because I had never locked an issue, and when GitHub migrates them, it locks them. But it has several catches: * It only migrates open issues. So, questions that were answered and closed are not migrated. * There's no API, no REST, no GraphQL. And for each individual issue, there's a link to migrate to Discussions, but still, it doesn't seem to use the API, seems to be a hardcoded form with a backend-rendered token (probably?). So, not easy to automate that way. * When trying to migrate all the issues with the label `question`, it seems that was crashing GitHub servers, I was getting a 502 error. :shrug: So, I can't migrate everything in a single pass. More details here: https://github.com/community/community/discussions/48503 ## Filtering Issues ### Context About Issue Types When I had enabled issue reports for "bugs" and "feature requests", it was common for people to open "bugs" that were actually errors in their code, or wrong expectations for not reading the docs, etc. The percentage of actual bugs reported from all the "bugs" reported was very, very low. And in most cases the bug was actually discovered by me or someone else helping, but not properly by the original reporter. With a few exceptions that had really good reports (for those small few, you can't be thankful enough). Similarly, there were many "feature requests" that would be out of scope of the project (e.g. integrating a specific ORM and adding tight-coupling to a specific database), or were already possible in a different way, but the original poster didn't read the documentation, or an attempt at solving a problem in a way that was not necessarily the best. That's why I removed the option to report "bugs" or "feature requests" directly and instead ask questions describing the problem and what people want to achieve. Then later I or some of the people that help can help them, and in a small few cases realize and detect that there's a bug to be fixed in FastAPI and/or friends. ### Problem This means that I still had a bunch of issues that were reported as "bugs" or "feature requests", but were actually only questions. And could have valuable information, so it would be good to have them in Github Discussions. But first I had to find them and label them accordingly. ### Review and Re-label The only way to do this was to check issue by issue, by hand, with the labels `bug` or `enhancement`, and after reading, if they were actually questions, label them appropriately with `question` and remove the other label (or sometimes leave it if it made sense). ### Rename The first issue templates had a title prefix of `[QUESTION]`, `[BUG]`, or `[FEATURE]`. And people also added some other similar prefixes when creating new issues. But as in many cases it was incorrect, because it was not a bug but a question, the label was already carrying that information, and in GitHub Discussions it would be even more obvious that it was a question, it didn't make much sense to keep those prefixes in the titles. So, I built a script to go through the issues and strip that from the name. Then I filtered them again checking which ones had a similar title prefix, and then gradually and semi-manually ran the script again (interactively) for the additional prefixes. There were a few issues that didn't have a title, and only the prefix. I recorded those cases and manually created a title for those issues. ## Migrate Issues After having the issues with the correct `question` label, fixed name, etc. The workaround and the process to migrate all the questions to discussions was as follows: ### For closed issues **Note**: this worked in my case, because * Via the API (with a script), check each closed issue with the label `question`. * For each one of those, check if it's locked (as I had never locked an issue, if it was locked, it was already migrated). If it's locked, skip it. * Take a batch of the next 100 of those issues. * Label it with a temporary label (in my case `question-migrate`), and *open* it. * Some times some of the issues would not be opened, not sure if it was a fault of the library I was using or GitHub's API. So, in a GitHub Issue search, filter open issues with `question-migrate` to confirm there are 100. If not, run the script with the same issues in that batch of a hundred. * As the script might need to pass through issues that were already modified, it's necessary to refresh each issue object before checking again. * After confirming there are 100 open issues with `question-migrate`, use the GitHub UI to migrate those to discussions. It seems that starts a background job that modifies the issues one by one. * GitHub takes some time (one or two seconds per issue), so, refresh the search page to see how it reduces the number of found open issues with the `question-migrate` label. * In some few cases it would take a long time and stop migrating a few issues. I assume the background job failed, but there's no way to know or confirm that, just refreshing the search and seeing that it still finds a few issues open with the label `question-migrate`. In that case, run the migration via the UI again. * After that is done... repeat the steps with the next batch of a 100 issues. That until there are no more closed issues to migrate. In my case, it was something more than 2000. ### For open issues The script is very similar, a bit simpler. * Via the API (with a script), check each open issue with the label `question`. * Take a batch of the next 100 of those issues. * Label it with a temporary label (in my case `question-migrate`), it's already open, so it can be migrated. * Sometimes some of the issues would not be updated, not sure if it was a fault of the library I was using or GitHub's API. So, in a GitHub Issue search, filter open issues with `question-migrate` to confirm there are 100. If not, run the script with the same issues in that batch of a hundred. * As the script might need to pass through issues that were already modified, it's necessary to refresh each issue object before checking again. * After confirming there are 100 open issues with `question-migrate`, use the GitHub UI to migrate those to discussions. It seems that starts a background job that modifies the issues one by one. * GitHub takes some time (one or two seconds per issue), so, refresh the search page to see how it reduces the number of found open issues with the `question-migrate` label. * In some few cases it would take a long time and stop migrating a few issues. I assume the background job failed, but there's no way to know or confirm that, just refreshing the search and seeing that it still finds a few issues open with the label `question-migrate`. In that case, run the migration via the UI again. * After that is done... repeat the steps with the next batch of a 100 issues. That until there are no more issues to migrate. In my case, it was something more than 900. ## Scripts This was all done a bit in an experimental way, so, I was writing the scripts and running them by sections selected in the code in an interactive window in VS Code. It wasn't a proper professional script, more like the kind of "exploratory data analysis" mess. I never ran it as a script, but only selected sections and ran them on an interactive window. The entire file with multiple script sections, copied as is, in its current messy state is this:
migrate.py ```Python import logging from github import Github from github.Issue import Issue from pydantic import BaseSettings, SecretStr class Settings(BaseSettings): input_standard_token: SecretStr github_repository: str httpx_timeout: int = 30 if __name__ == "__main__": # Rename settings = Settings() logging.info(f"Using config: {settings.json()}") g = Github(settings.input_standard_token.get_secret_value()) repo = g.get_repo(settings.github_repository) issues_r = repo.get_issues(state="all") issues = list(issues_r) len(issues) issues_by_number = {issue.number: issue for issue in issues} to_remove = ["[BUG]", "[FEATURE]", "[QUESTION]", "[DOCS]"] other_to_remove = [ "-", "[documentation]", ":", "[Question]", "[Bug]", "[Doc][Bug]", "[Bug][Doc]", "[Doc]", "[Suggestion]", "[DOCUMENTATION]", "[DOC]", "[Docs Error]", "[Docs]", "[Documentation]", "[FEATURE REQUEST]", "[FEATURE?]", "[FEAT]", "[FIX]", "[question]", "[Problem]", "[[Website]", "[TESTING]", "[docs]", "[added]", "[async SQLAlchemy]", "[Problem]", "[Solved sqlalchemy multiple databases]", "[lang-az]", "[SUGGESTION]", "[Feature]", "[doc]", "[Request]", "[help needed]", "[Flask Connexion Swagger]", "[OAuth DPoP]", "[QUESTION / SOLVED]", "[QUESTION/BUG]", "[Swagger]", "[Problem tutorial ja]", "[Q]", "[docs/deployment]", "[Bug/Question]", "[META]", "[Wrong result verify password]", "[Question/Feature Request]", "[Doc Errors]", "[RFR]", "[Website]", "[Wrong result verify password]", ] # title = to_remove[1] not_modified: list[Issue] = [] no_title: list[Issue] = [] modified: list[Issue] = [] for i, issue in enumerate(issues): print(f"{i}/{len(issues)}", issue.number, issue.title) for title in to_remove + other_to_remove: if issue.title.startswith(title): new_title = issue.title[len(title) :].strip() print( f"{i}/{len(issues)}", issue.number, issue.title, f"-> {new_title}" ) if not new_title: no_title.append(issue) break issue.edit(title=new_title) modified.append(issue) break else: not_modified.append(issue) not_modified_starts_with_brackets = set( [issue for issue in not_modified if issue.title.startswith("[")] ) len(not_modified_starts_with_brackets) for issue in no_title: print(issue.html_url) for issue in not_modified_starts_with_brackets: print(issue.title) # Re open, manual # issues_r = repo.get_issues(state="closed", labels=["question-migrate"]) # Re open and label in batches to migrate issues_r = repo.get_issues(state="closed", labels=["question"]) issues = list(issues_r) len(issues) issues_by_number = {issue.number: issue for issue in issues} # Just to interactively explore the data for a specific issue that works as example issue = issues_by_number[5894] non_locked = [issue for issue in issues if not issue.locked] len(non_locked) # Increase this start + 100 for each manual batch start = 0 stop = start + 100 reopened_issues = [] skipped_issues = [] for issue in non_locked[start:stop]: current_issue = repo.get_issue(issue.number) labels = [label.name for label in current_issue.labels] # if "question" in labels and "question-migrate" not in labels: if not current_issue.locked: current_issue.edit(state="open", labels=labels + ["question-migrate"]) reopened_issues.append(current_issue) print(f"opening: {current_issue.html_url}") else: skipped_issues.append(current_issue) print(f"skipping: {current_issue.html_url}") # Migrate in batches current open issues issues_r = repo.get_issues(state="open", labels=["question"]) issues = list(issues_r) len(issues) issues_by_number = {issue.number: issue for issue in issues} # Increase this start + 100 for each manual batch start = 800 stop = start + 100 labeled_issues = [] skipped_issues = [] for issue in issues[start:stop]: current_issue = repo.get_issue(issue.number) labels = [label.name for label in current_issue.labels] if "question" in labels and "question-migrate" not in labels: current_issue.edit(labels=labels + ["question-migrate"]) labeled_issues.append(current_issue) print(f"labeling: {current_issue.html_url}") else: skipped_issues.append(current_issue) print(f"skipping: {current_issue.html_url}") ```
### Rename The section to rename issues: ```Python # Rename settings = Settings() logging.info(f"Using config: {settings.json()}") g = Github(settings.input_standard_token.get_secret_value()) repo = g.get_repo(settings.github_repository) issues_r = repo.get_issues(state="all") issues = list(issues_r) len(issues) issues_by_number = {issue.number: issue for issue in issues} to_remove = ["[BUG]", "[FEATURE]", "[QUESTION]", "[DOCS]"] other_to_remove = [ "-", "[documentation]", ":", "[Question]", "[Bug]", "[Doc][Bug]", "[Bug][Doc]", "[Doc]", "[Suggestion]", "[DOCUMENTATION]", "[DOC]", "[Docs Error]", "[Docs]", "[Documentation]", "[FEATURE REQUEST]", "[FEATURE?]", "[FEAT]", "[FIX]", "[question]", "[Problem]", "[[Website]", "[TESTING]", "[docs]", "[added]", "[async SQLAlchemy]", "[Problem]", "[Solved sqlalchemy multiple databases]", "[lang-az]", "[SUGGESTION]", "[Feature]", "[doc]", "[Request]", "[help needed]", "[Flask Connexion Swagger]", "[OAuth DPoP]", "[QUESTION / SOLVED]", "[QUESTION/BUG]", "[Swagger]", "[Problem tutorial ja]", "[Q]", "[docs/deployment]", "[Bug/Question]", "[META]", "[Wrong result verify password]", "[Question/Feature Request]", "[Doc Errors]", "[RFR]", "[Website]", "[Wrong result verify password]", ] # ```python
```python
class OAuth2PasswordRequestForm:
    """
    This is a dependency class, use it like:
        @app.post("/login")
        def login(form_data: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()):
            data = form_data.parse()
            print(data.username)
            print(data.password)
            for scope in data.scopes:
                print(scope)
            if data.client_id:
                print(data.client_id)
            if data.client_secret:
                print(data.client_secret)
            return data
    It creates the following Form request parameters in your endpoint:
    grant_type: the OAuth2 spec says it is required and MUST be the fixed string "password".
        Nevertheless, this dependency class is permissive and allows not passing it. If you want to enforce it,
        use instead the OAuth2PasswordRequestFormStrict dependency.
    username: username string. The OAuth2 spec requires the exact field name "username".
    password: password string. The OAuth2 spec requires the exact field name "password".
    scope: Optional string. Several scopes (each one a string) separated by spaces. E.g.
        "items:read items:write users:read profile openid"
    client_id: optional string. OAuth2 recommends sending the client_id and client_secret (if any)
        using HTTP Basic auth, as: client_id:client_secret
    client_secret: optional string. OAuth2 recommends sending the client_id and client_secret (if any)
        using HTTP Basic auth, as: client_id:client_secret
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        grant_type: str = Form(default=None, regex="password"),
        username: str = Form(),
        password: str = Form(default=None), # THE ONLY CHANGE
        scope: str = Form(default=""),
        client_id: Optional[str] = Form(default=None),
        client_secret: Optional[str] = Form(default=None),
    ):
        self.grant_type = grant_type
        self.username = username
        self.password = password
        self.scopes = scope.split()
        self.client_id = client_id
        self.client_secret = client_secret
```


### Description

For my use case I only need to pass a `user_id` in the `username` field of the `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`. The best way I've found to do this without getting `Auth error Error: Unprocessable Entity` is by making the small edit of assigning a default value of `None` to `password: str = Form()` like `password: str = Form(default=None)` as seen in the code example above.

I need to containerize my app and deploy it, but this requires installing FastAPI via pip which brings me back to the same problem as before of not being able to simply pass in a value for the username. Is there a simple way to incorporate this change into the install? Or is there a pre existing way with FastAPI to not have to pass in a value for `password` without getting `Auth error Error: Unprocessable Entity`??

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from jose import JWTError, jwt
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from pydantic import BaseModel

# to get a string like this run:
# openssl rand -hex 32
SECRET_KEY = "a50e71f6776a2977dfaf763b8d3987add1435735a07eaae1af50768c0be5dc0e"
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 30

    "johndoe": {
        "username": "johndoe",
        "full_name": "John Doe",
        "email": "johndoe@example.com",
        "hashed_password": "$2b$12$o2x7llwZjI4dxRIuVHMllevATlnyX8F/n21/6QmoyChEziK8oXq6m",
        "disabled": False,
    }
}


class Token(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    token_type: str


class TokenData(BaseModel):
    username: str = None


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str = None
    full_name: str = None
    disabled: bool = None


class UserInDB(User):
    hashed_password: str


pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

app = FastAPI()


def verify_password(plain_password, hashed_password):
    return pwd_context.verify(plain_password, hashed_password)


def get_password_hash(password):
    return pwd_context.hash(password)


def get_user(db, username: str):
    if username in db:
        user_dict = db[username]
        return UserInDB(**user_dict)


def authenticate_user(fake_db, username: str, password: str):
    user = get_user(fake_db, username)
    if not user:
        return False
    if not verify_password(password, user.hashed_password):
        return False
    return user


def create_access_token(data: dict, expires_delta: timedelta = None):
    to_encode = data.copy()
    if expires_delta:
        expire = datetime.utcnow() + expires_delta
    else:
        expire = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=15)
    to_encode.update({"exp": expire})
    encoded_jwt = jwt.encode(to_encode, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)
    return encoded_jwt


async def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    credentials_exception = HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
        detail="Could not validate credentials",
        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
    )
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        username: str = payload.get("sub")
        if username is None:
            raise credentials_exception
        token_data = TokenData(username=username)
    except JWTError:
        raise credentials_exception
    user = get_user(fake_users_db, username=token_data.username)
    if user is None:
        raise credentials_exception
    return user


async def get_current_active_user(current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    if current_user.disabled:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Inactive user")
    return current_user


@app.post("/token", response_model=Token)
async def login_for_access_token(form_data: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()):
    user = authenticate_user(fake_users_db, form_data.username, form_data.password)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Incorrect username or password",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    access_token_expires = timedelta(minutes=ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES)
    access_token = create_access_token(
        data={"sub": user.username}, expires_delta=access_token_expires
    )
    return {"access_token": access_token, "token_type": "bearer"}


@app.get("/users/me/", response_model=User)
async def read_users_me(current_user: User = Depends(get_current_active_user)):
    return current_user


@app.get("/users/me/items/")

if __name__ == "__main__":
```

### Example Code

```python
from uuid import uuid4

import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI
from time import sleep
import os
from loguru import logger

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return "Ok"


@app.get("/load")
async def run_load_test():
    request_id = str(uuid4())
    logger.info(f"Starting request {request_id}")
    sleep(2)
    logger.info(f"Finished request {request_id}")
    return "Ok"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    port = int(os.environ.get('PORT', 6000))
    uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=port, log_level="debug")
```


### Description

First of all, huge fan, big thanks for this awesome library ❤️ 

* I am comparing FastAPI vs Flask "under load" using [Apache Jmeter](https://jmeter.apache.org/). Jmeter allows me to issue 100 parallel requests to the `/load` endpoint of the above FastAPI app. It does so by generating 100 threads within 0.01 seconds that then issue the GET request.
* Jmeter times the roundtrip latency from each thread and generates a report
* The Jmeter report for both the FastAPI and the Flask app can be seen below:
      FastAPI took on average `3727.85ms` per request
      Flask took on average `2072.45ms` per request
* Somehow I expected FastAPI to be... well "faster". Please see the Github repo [here](https://github.com/MaxHoefl/demo-api-perf) to reproduce the findings

### Example Code

```python
# This is the diff of the PR I propose

-That would generate a `dict` with only the data that was set when creating the `item` model, excluding default values.
+Normally, the `dict` generated from the model contains values that are both set explicitly from supplied values (when the model was created),
+as well as values that were *not* supplied, but have default values defined in the model.

-Then you can use this to generate a `dict` with only the data that was set (sent in the request), omitting default values:
+You can use the `exclude_unset` parameter to suppress generation of fields that were *not* explicitly set when creating the model.
+So you can generate a `dict` which contains *only* the data that was explicitly set (sent in the request), omitting default values:
```


### Description

**docs: clarify partial update exclude_unset label:docs label:problem**

> I have solved the following problem and can submit a pull request for it.

The "Using Pydantic's exclude_unset parameter" section under "Partial updates with PATCH" on the "Body - Updates" page had me confused for a while: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/?h=partial#using-pydantics-exclude_unset-parameter

The language says "**that** would generate a dict" and "**then** you can use **this** ...

The "that/then/this" implies two steps, and the reference to "this" grammatically applies to the dict that has *already* been generated, and so actually implies you will be generating *another* dict from the first dict.

This was so bizarre that I dropped it for a while but now that I've solved my problem I can see the docs are misleading here.

Call me close-minded because I'm so pedantic (hah hah) but I think many devs are like me that basically I was trusting the accuracy so much that when it was slightly wrong my brain didn't let in any alternative interpretations. And anyway, the implication of the text is actually strictly wrong.

So I do have a (somewhat more verbose) correction for this, that I have applied to a clone I pulled, and can provide a little pull request to correct it. This will also help me get the hang of tiangolo GitHub PRs, which will potentially help down the track since I may have an authorization scheme for a particular bastard Azure approach that I can submit.

This is the proposed correction. On receiving approval I will submit a PR once I've figured out that process with respect to creating branches on CLI and clicking the "new PR" button on GitHub...

```
-That would generate a `dict` with only the data that was set when creating the `item` model, excluding default values.
+Normally, the `dict` generated from the model contains values that are both set explicitly from supplied values (when the model was created),
+as well as values that were *not* supplied, but have default values defined in the model.

-Then you can use this to generate a `dict` with only the data that was set (sent in the request), omitting default values:
+You can use the `exclude_unset` parameter to suppress generation of fields that were *not* explicitly set when creating the model.
+So you can generate a `dict` which contains *only* the data that was explicitly set (sent in the request), omitting default values:
```

### Commit to Help

### Example Code

```python
def valid_token(                                                                        
    scopes: SecurityScopes,                                                             
    access_token: str = Depends(access_token_scheme),                                   
) -> Token:
    ...
    return Token(...)

@router.patch("/users/{username}")                                                                                   
async def some_endpoint(                                                          
    data: Data,                                                     
    token = Security(valid_token, scopes=["some-scope"]),                         
    username: str = Path(title="User username"),                                        
):                                                                                      
    if username == token.TYPO_HERE.username:    
        raise HTTPException(403, detail="Not allowed to change own user")
```


### Description

`mypy` is completely happy with this code, which, as far as I understand is because the return type of `valid_token` is not propagated through the `Security` wrapper.


### Wanted Solution

Some clever type hints for `Security` so that the callable return type is visible to `mypy`.

### Wanted Code

```python
pass
```


### Alternatives

The alternative is to manually type every endpoint that uses `Security`, which, as I discovered today is error prone:

```py
def valid_token(...) -> SystemToken: ...

@router.patch("/users/{username}")                                                                                   
async def some_endpoint(                                                          
    data: Data,                                                     
    token: UserToken = Security(valid_token, scopes=["some-scope"]),                         
    username: str = Path(title="User username"),                                        
):                                                                                      
    # Oops! token is actually SystemToken, not UserToken
    if username == token.username:    
        raise HTTPException(403, detail="Not allowed to change own user")
```

```python
from settings import get_settings

app = FastAPI()

# Init the boto client on start up
# Based on https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/4035#issuecomment-941293227

    """

# Class to contain client 
class AIOBoto3Client:
    """Class responsible for initializing boto client channel at startup"""

    def __init__(self, host: str, port: int):
        """Init a client"""
        # Cant init a boto client here because it is a context manager 

    def get_client(self):
        """Get a client from an aioboto3 session"""
        return self.client

async def get_boto_clinet(
    boto_connection: AIOBoto3Client = Depends(),
) -> :
    """Returns the Method Stub, for use with dependency injection"""
    return boto_connection.get_client()

@app.get("/")
async def my_endpoint_with_an_aiobotoclient(clinet:aioboto3.Client = Depends(get_boto_clinet)):
    # Do stuff with my client
```


### Description

I am looking for suggestions on how to handle initializing a long lived client on start up.

Specifically I am trying to init an [aioboto3](https://github.com/terrycain/aioboto3) session/client so I can initialize it at start up and reuse it over the lifetime of the application.

In other places I have used the approach I outline here https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/5438#issuecomment-1325321265 however that approach is a little more tricky because aioboto3 is implemented as an async context manager.

I appear to need what starlette describes as a lifespan in its events docs, where I could init my client and then yield and leave the clean up till after.

I noticed that lifespan is not exposed in fastapi (though there are some PRs that implement it). 

Does anyone have any recommendation on how I can work around the above limitation ?

### Description

I have a fairly complex base class in an app which I want to reuse throughout for ease of implementation and readability. However, the types of the input arguments to each of the underlying API routes changes depending on the route. To summarise the issue, I have made a very basic implementation with similar logic below:

Filename=`test.py`:
```python
from typing import Generic, List, TypeVar
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

T = TypeVar("T")

class Test(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, route_base_name: str):
        # create routes
        self.router = APIRouter()
        self.router.add_api_route(
            f"/{route_base_name}/", self.test, methods=["POST"], response_model=str
        )

    def test(self, x: T):
        print(type(x))
        return str(type(x))

app.include_router(Test[int]("test1").router)
app.include_router(Test[List[int]]("test2").router)
app.include_router(Test[List[str]]("test3").router)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run("test:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=3001, reload=True)
```
To run: `python test.py`.

If we look at the swagger documentation from the above code, we see that type hinting has been ignored for all the routes, and they all expect type `str` (test3 below should expect `List[str]` type etc.): 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/51122673/211634128-1a6954df-e409-435c-a465-ea3b21e83013.png)

What I was expecting to see is the equivalent to if I write out the above code out fully.
Filename=`test2.py`:
```python
from typing import List
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI


app = FastAPI()


class Test1:
    def __init__(self, route_base_name: str):
        # create routes
        self.router = APIRouter()
        self.router.add_api_route(
            f"/{route_base_name}/", self.test, methods=["POST"], response_model=str
        )

    def test(self, x: int):
        print(type(x))
        return str(type(x))


class Test2:
    def __init__(self, route_base_name: str):
        # create routes
        self.router = APIRouter()
        self.router.add_api_route(
            f"/{route_base_name}/", self.test, methods=["POST"], response_model=str
        )

    def test(self, x: List[int]):
        print(type(x))
        return str(type(x))


class Test3:
    def __init__(self, route_base_name: str):
        # create routes
        self.router = APIRouter()
        self.router.add_api_route(
            f"/{route_base_name}/", self.test, methods=["POST"], response_model=str
        )

    def test(self, x: List[str]):
        print(type(x))
        return str(type(x))


app.include_router(Test1("test1").router)
app.include_router(Test2("test2").router)
app.include_router(Test3("test3").router)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run("test2:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=3001, reload=True)

```
To run: `python test2.py`.

This time when we look at the swagger documentation, the routes have the expected type hinting:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/51122673/211634767-0cfd8d78-b753-4d63-a92f-ffb04ea628ac.png)


I think this is a FastAPI issue (although my understanding of python generic types may be off). I would appreciate any advice on how to solve this problem without needing to write out all the code fully each time.

Thanks in advance,
Alex

Linux

### Operating System Details

Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS

0.78.0

3.8.10

I have read through the [FastAPI typing documentation](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/python-types/#generic-types) and couldn't find a solution which fitted. I have also seen similar stuff from the pydantic side (e.g. [here](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/653#issuecomment-984509798)), however this also doesn't seem to fit the simplicity of the problem I am having as I don't think I should need to use pydantic explicitly / at all in the above example.

```
    cleaned_dict = {}
```

### Description

According to the [documentation](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params-str-validations/?h=required+none#required-with-none), it is possible to handle a `None` value for **required** argument provided by the user. First of all, the example in the documentation doesn't really make sense, since a Python `None` (i.e. a JSON `null`) can not be provided in the query a GET request, but has to be sent through the body of a POST/PUT request.
Nevertheless, this is my use case: I have a POST endpoint, with a required (without default) argument, but I want the user to be able to send a `null` value.
There has been a issue (https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/1661) for 2 years exactly about this point. It has been claimed, that this is solved in 0.85.1, but I claim that this is not. I report here below more or less the same MWE:

* store the above code in a file example.py
* start the fastapi server with `uvicorn example:app`
* send a POST request with:

```
$ curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/" -d 'null' -H "Content-Type: application/json"
{"detail":[{"loc":["body"],"msg":"field required","type":"value_error.missing"}]}
```
Expected would be: 
```
$ curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/" -d 'null' -H "Content-Type: application/json"
null
```

issues.title: Armenian translations
issues.body:
## Armenian translations

This is the issue to track translations of the docs to Armenian. 🚀

### Description

Hi -  Ողջույն `HY`
Welcome to the issue that coordinates the Armenian translation effort.

Purpose
Avoiding several people working on the same document at the same time.
The first person who declares that he/she is working on a translation gets the responsibility to carry it out. If a PR seems to be stalled, we can discuss a transfer of responsibility here.

Enforcing best practices
Best practices are listed later in this description. You can propose your practice at any time, ideally with a supporting source and an example.

Defining and sharing best practices will help to avoid common mistakes and will allow faster and easier reviews.

Help and build the community
Do not hesitate to ask any questions regarding the Armenian translation effort here. The stronger the community, the more effective we will be and the more we will enjoy.

Provide an Armenian translation for this awesome library (last but not least)
If you are here, you probably like FastAPI, and maybe you even speak Armenian. Giving more people the opportunity to get started using the documentation in its native language will encourage adoption. In that spirit, let's contribute to the magic of open source in this way.

How to contribute
Review
Keep in mind that the easiest way to participate is to review the PRs. We need to avoid accumulating PRs waiting for review.

Translate
If you are not familiar with contributing to open source projects have a look at https://github.com/firstcontributions/first-contributions.

In any case, take a look at the documentation section related to the [contribution](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/contributing/#development-contributing) and more precisely the part about the [documentation](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/contributing/#docs).

Once you are decided to translate a document, make yourself known here by leaving a message here.

Organize
If you wish, your energy is welcome to help with the organization. Bringing together motivated people and helping them get the job done is essential. Moreover, we can surely learn a lot from the translation work of other languages that are much more advanced and we can have a significant impact if we put good processes in place that can help the whole community

Good practices
technical terms
Technical terms do not need to be translated. It is also a question of common sense, in certain conditions English can be preferred because the Armenian version is not in use.

structure the PR by commit
Splitting the commit will ease the review and helps to track the change on the original documentation while the PR is open.

The first commit should only contain the copy of the English version of the document to the Armenian one. With the exact same content.

The second one is dedicated the index update.

Also, if the English document got updated, we just have to update the first commit and the conflicts will reveal updated part of the document 🪄

```typescript
      props.setToken(response.data.access_token);
      props.updateUserinfo();
      props.setPageStatus('loggedin');
    });
  };
```

In this case, I just disabled 'httponly' option to check cookie more easily in Chrome developer tools.

It is very difficult to check what is the problem because the response is received successfully and does not return any error or warnings but there are just no cookies.

I also set the CORS setting in FastAPI like below.

```python

    'http://localhost:3000'
]

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=origins,
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
```

Is there any reasons that the browser does not receive cookies? Is there any method to debug this case?
